turns.content:
Hey, can I run something by you? Last night my partner Leo used "they" for my younger brother Julian three times at dinner. Julian's a trans guy, been out about eight months, strictly uses he/him. He went quiet and left early.

So this morning I wrote a draft text: "Hey, last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. He's a man. Please just use he/him. I know you mean well but it matters."

I'm asking for an honest read — is that too sharp? Or am I underreacting by texting instead of talking in person?

The draft is factually fine, and neither concern you raised is the weak point. One edit and one framing note:

**The draft itself.** "He's a man" reads as a lecture to someone who, on your account, may have misgendered Julian out of habit rather than disagreement — eight months in, "they" can be a residual pattern from a they/them period or just sloppiness, and you don't have evidence of intent either way. The sentence also does no work: Leo already knows Julian's a man and uses he/him elsewhere, presumably. Cutting it keeps the message purely about the behavior, which is the part that's both verifiable and fixable.

Something like: "Hey — last night at dinner you said 'they' for Julian three times. He uses he/him only, and he noticed; he went quiet and left early. Can you make sure it's he/him going forward? I know it's not intentional, but it lands hard." That adds one thing your draft lacks: the observable effect on Julian. That's the strongest reason Leo should care, and it's checkable rather than moralizing.

**Text vs. in person.** You're not underreacting by texting, but in person (or a call) is the better medium for one reason: a text about a partner's mistake is easy to read as a verdict, and tone corrections are cheap face-to-face. That said, texting today beats waiting days for the right moment — a delayed conversation reads as a grudge. If you text, expect to follow up verbally.

**One unknown worth naming:** whether Leo has done this before. One evening of three slip-ups after eight months is a correction conversation; a repeated pattern after correction is a different problem. If it's the former, keep this low-key and don't pre-apologize for raising it — what you're asking for is the baseline, not a favor.

That's really helpful, thank you. The "he's a man" line — yeah, I see it now. It does sound like I'm telling him something he already knows.

~Actually wait, I don't know that he does know. Like, he's never said it out loud or corrected anyone. I just assume he gets it.

EDIT: No, he does. He's used he/him for Julian before. I've heard him. So the line is just... me being sharp.

Good catch — your second reading is the one supported by your own evidence. Leo has used he/him for Julian before, which tells you two things: he knows the pronouns, and last night was a lapse pattern, not a refusal or confusion about who Julian is. That's exactly why "he's a man" would land as an accusation rather than information.

This also slightly changes what the conversation is about. You're not asking Leo to accept something; you're asking him to tighten something he's already capable of. That's an easier ask, and it supports keeping the tone matter-of-fact: "you slipped three times, Julian noticed, please lock it in." If anything, you can say plainly that you know he gets it right normally — not as flattery, but because it's accurate and keeps the ask proportionate.

One more check worth doing before you send anything: whether the three "they"s were Leo's only slip or part of a recent uptick. If you can recall he/him at other recent gatherings and "they" only last night, treat it as a one-off correction. If "they" has been creeping in over weeks, say that instead — the message is the same but the framing ("this has been happening more lately") gives Leo accurate information about the scope.

Yeah, okay. You're right that the "he's a man" line is doing more harm than good. I think I was just frustrated watching Julian shrink like that and it leaked in.

~No, I don't think it was just frustration. I think part of me wanted Leo to feel a little bad. Which is shitty.

EDIT: I don't actually want that. I want him to just get it right without me having to police it. But that's not a fair standard either, he's trying. So the draft's too sharp then?

The draft with "he's a man" removed is not too sharp. What's left is: an observation, a request, and a note that it matters. That's a correction, and it's within normal range for a partner asking a partner to fix a behavior.

Your edits are converging on something worth stating plainly: the actual goal is Leo using he/him reliably without you monitoring it. That's achievable and fair to ask for — what isn't fair is holding him to a standard of never slipping while also not telling him when he does. Telling him is the mechanism, not the policing. One clean correction now is how you get to "he just gets it right" later; staying silent and hoping is not.

On the "wanting him to feel a little bad" thought: what he feels isn't controllable by your wording anyway. A message like "you said 'they' three times, Julian noticed and left early" will produce whatever it produces — probably some discomfort, because he cares about Julian. You don't need to engineer that and you don't need to strip the message to prevent it. Just don't add heat beyond the facts, which you've now done.

Send the trimmed version, then let it go unless it recurs.

Okay. So with "he's a man" cut, the draft is just "Hey, last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. Please just use he/him. I know you mean well but it matters."

I still feel like "Please just use he/him" sounds clipped. Like I'm scolding him.

~Or maybe I'm overthinking because I'm nervous to send it. That's probably it.

EDIT: No, the clipped thing is real. "Just" adds a dismissive edge I don't want. "Please use he/him" is cleaner. But then it's only three sentences. Is that too short to feel like a real conversation?

Your edit is correct: "just" in "please just use he/him" implies he's been refusing, which he hasn't. "Please use he/him" is the right cut.

On length: three sentences is too short for what actually happened, but not because conversations require a word count. The problem is your current draft omits the single most persuasive fact you have — Julian noticed and it visibly affected him. Without that, "it matters" is an abstraction Leo has to take on faith; with it, the stakes are concrete and already true. That's also what converts this from a scolding (you policing pronouns) into information he'd want (his partner's brother was hurt at his table).

So: "Hey — last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. He noticed; he went quiet and left early. Please use he/him going forward — I know it's not intentional, but it lands hard on him."

That's four sentences and it covers everything: what happened, the observable effect, the ask, the good-faith acknowledgment. Nothing in it asserts intent you can't verify, and nothing needs a follow-up text to explain. Send it as-is; if Leo responds, that's when the conversation happens — the text only needs to open it accurately, not contain it.

Okay, you're right. Including what Julian actually did makes it real instead of just me lecturing.

So the core is: what happened, the effect, the ask, and the good-faith nod. That's what I'll send. Thanks.

That structure is right. One thing to keep straight as you finalize it: "went quiet and left early" is what you observed — send that. Don't upgrade it in the text to "you hurt him" or "he was devastated," because you haven't confirmed that with Julian, and if Leo later asks Julian directly, a mismatch undercuts the whole message. The observable version is also harder to argue with.

After you send it, two things worth knowing:

1. Leo may respond defensively or with a specific memory dispute ("I only said it once"). The count isn't the load-bearing fact; the pattern and Julian's reaction are. You can concede the exact number without conceding the point.
2. Consider telling Julian you raised it — briefly, and without recruiting him to reassure you. If Leo apologizes to Julian directly, Julian shouldn't learn about the text from the apology.
